stories.question: In Plato's Republic, does the philosopher‑king's rule preserve justice or betray individual freedom when 'the good' is known by a few?
stories.rationale: Plato (Republic) constructs an elite political order justified by knowledge of the Good, creating a tension between collective justice and individual autonomy. Readers dispute whether the philosopher‑king's authority is paternalistic or legitimately necessary for a just polis. Use weak performance signals (see X post id 304; source_grid_id: philosophical-themes-in-a-separation-asghar-farha-1caa1c) as directional evidence that politically framed tensions engage audiences (not proof). Metric/grid IDs: X id 304; source_grid_id: philosophical-themes-in-a-separation-asghar-farha-1caa1c.

stories.question: In Kant's Groundwork, can strict duty and universalisable maxims coexist with neighbourly compassion when moral law seems to forbid exceptions?
stories.rationale: Kant (Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals) insists on duty derived from universal reason; critics highlight a tension where inflexible maxims appear to outlaw acts of compassion that require exceptions. Competing interpretations treat Kant as permitting particularised duties via practical reason or as mandating rigid obedience. Weak evidence: LinkedIn post id 65 showed interest in Popper/Kantian truth debates (sample signal only). Metric/grid IDs: LinkedIn id 65; source_grid_id: karl-poppers-source-of-knowledge-and-ignorance-10d92f.

stories.question: Does Mill's On Liberty protect individuality at the cost of tolerating social harms when free expression entrenches inequality?
stories.rationale: John Stuart Mill (On Liberty) champions liberty as essential to individuality and progress, yet tolerant policies can perpetuate harms and power imbalances—raising an internal conflict between liberty and protective regulation. This is a familiar editorial hook with modest engagement in platform data (see Facebook id 1366; source_grid_id: how-does-bullshit-jobs-a-theory-by-david-graeber-i-5e433b). Metric/grid IDs: Facebook id 1366; source_grid_id: how-does-bullshit-jobs-a-theory-by-david-graeber-i-5e433b.

stories.question: In Thus Spoke Zarathustra, can Nietzsche teach self-overcoming without turning his followers into another herd?
stories.rationale:
Nietzsche (Thus Spoke Zarathustra) praises self‑overcoming and the Übermensch while critics argue this ideal can undermine communal bonds and lead to domination. Scholarly readings disagree whether Nietzsche is emancipatory or proto‑elitist. Weak signal: TikTok exposure to Nietzsche/Russell style pieces suggests bite‑sized philosophical prompts can land (TikTok id 1590; source_grid_id: in-praise-of-idleness-bertrand-russell-308e9a). Metric/grid IDs: TikTok id 1590; source_grid_id: in-praise-of-idleness-bertrand-russell-308e9a.

Editorial source check: Use the tension between Zarathustra’s teaching and his demand that disciples find their own way, especially On the Bestowing Virtue. Avoid treating self-overcoming as a licence to dominate other people. Primary text: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/1998

stories.question: In Crime and Punishment, why does Raskolnikov’s theory of extraordinary people collapse when he tries to live by it?
stories.rationale:
Fyodor Dostoevsky (Crime and Punishment) stages Raskolnikov's theory‑action divide: are his crimes judged by abstract moral law or explained away by poverty, alienation and psychological torment? The novel supports divergent readings about blame and social causation. Weak platform evidence: YouTube posts on moral/meaningful music and culture drew large exposures, indicating narrative ethical questions can engage (YouTube id 1732; source_grid_id: why-is-the-band-joy-division-so-revered-731d04). Metric/grid IDs: YouTube id 1732; source_grid_id: why-is-the-band-joy-division-so-revered-731d04.

Editorial source check: Ground the exploration in Raskolnikov’s article, his conversation with Porfiry, his crime and its psychological aftermath. Preserve the novel’s tension between an intellectual justification and lived responsibility; poverty is context, not an automatic excuse. Primary text: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2554

stories.question: In The Second Sex, how can Beauvoir call for freedom when society shapes the person who chooses?
stories.rationale:
Simone de Beauvoir (The Second Sex) blends existentialist autonomy with a feminist account of material and social dependence; interpreters debate whether her account secures authentic freedom or shows it as structurally compromised. Weak evidence: Instagram posts on social dependence and specialisation show topical appetite (Instagram id 1441; source_grid_id: the-division-of-labour-and-race-to-the-bottom-of-e-ae93f6). Metric/grid IDs: Instagram id 1441; source_grid_id: the-division-of-labour-and-race-to-the-bottom-of-e-ae93f6.

Editorial source check: Focus on situated freedom, becoming rather than an innate destiny, and material conditions. Do not portray Beauvoir as saying social constraints erase agency or that freedom is simply willpower. Reference: The Second Sex, Introduction and Conclusion.

stories.question: In Eichmann in Jerusalem, why does Arendt’s account of thoughtlessness leave personal guilt intact?
stories.rationale:
Hannah Arendt (Eichmann in Jerusalem) coined 'the banality of evil' to diagnose ordinary thoughtlessness in bureaucratic atrocity; scholars dispute whether this mitigates individual guilt or heightens responsibility to think critically. Weak platform cue: LinkedIn interest in 'who counts' and political responsibility indicates civic moral puzzles resonate (LinkedIn id 467; source_grid_id: why-do-politicians-not-act-for-the-benefit-of-all-3e260e). Metric/grid IDs: LinkedIn id 467; source_grid_id: why-do-politicians-not-act-for-the-benefit-of-all-3e260e.

Editorial source check: Distinguish Arendt’s interpretation of thoughtlessness from exoneration or a claim that atrocities are trivial. Her portrayal of Eichmann remains contested; do not present it as an uncontested historical diagnosis. Primary reporting: https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/1963/02/16/eichmann-in-jerusalem-i

stories.question: In Marx’s Capital, why can a machine that saves labour make people work harder or longer?
stories.rationale:
Karl Marx (Capital) offers a systemic critique of capitalism and alienation; interpreters differ on whether his emphasis on collective emancipation can accommodate plural individual flourishing or tends toward instrumental collectivism. Weak signal: X posts about free will and societal constraints show engagement with systemic freedom themes (X id 1670; source_grid_id: free-will-might-be-an-illusion-based-on-recent-neu-75df12). Metric/grid IDs: X id 1670; source_grid_id: free-will-might-be-an-illusion-based-on-recent-neu-75df12.

Editorial source check: Use Capital Volume I, Chapter 15: productive capacity can reduce necessary labour, while capitalist incentives can extend or intensify work. Distinguish a possible use of technology from a claim that every invention always worsens life. Primary text: https://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1867-c1/ch15.htm

stories.question: In Mrs Dalloway, does Clarissa’s party overcome loneliness or hide it behind perfect manners?
stories.rationale:
Virginia Woolf (Mrs Dalloway) uses interior narration to generate moments of cross‑character empathy while also emphasising deep solitude; this editorial experiment tests whether audiences prefer questions framed around literary interiority as emotional versus political. Weak evidence: Instagram and Facebook posts about comfort, freedom and interior life had low but present exposures (Instagram id 1907; Facebook weaker example id 15). Metric/grid IDs: Instagram id 1907; Facebook id 15; note: labelled explicitly as 'Editorial experiment' to trial format/engagement.

Editorial source check: Editorial experiment: a recognisable novel and concrete social scene, rather than an abstract political binary. Ground the discussion in Clarissa’s hosting, private recollection and encounters. Treat possible readings as interpretations. Avoid romanticising suicide or reproducing method details. Primary text: Virginia Woolf, Mrs Dalloway.

stories.question: In Being and Nothingness, why is Sartre’s waiter in bad faith if he really is a waiter?
stories.rationale:
Jean‑Paul Sartre (Being and Nothingness) equates existence with radical freedom and responsibility; debates centre on whether this freedom is liberating or condemning because it leaves individuals alone to create value under social pressure. Weak platform cue: LinkedIn post on 'Hell is Other People — Sartre' drew modest attention (LinkedIn id 1503; source_grid_id: hell-is-other-people-sartre-dccaba). Metric/grid IDs: LinkedIn id 1503; source_grid_id: hell-is-other-people-sartre-dccaba.

Editorial source check: Use Sartre’s café waiter to explore the tension between having a real social role and treating that role as a complete fixed identity. Preserve facticity and real constraints; freedom is not an ability to do anything. Primary text: Being and Nothingness, Part One, Chapter Two, Bad Faith.

theme:
Focus on famous books and named thinkers, rather than general ideas. Every question must name a specific recognisable book or thinker and expose an interesting internal tension, apparent contradiction, or serious argument in that work. Aim for a varied, accessible selection across philosophy and classic literature: freedom versus responsibility, compassion versus duty, revolt versus meaning, authenticity versus social dependence, and similar concrete human conflicts. Do not cover AI. Avoid repeating previous grids. Use recent performance as weak evidence and include one clearly labelled editorial experiment. Ground each question in the actual text or thinker; preserve competing interpretations, do not invent quotations or biographical claims, and identify the work in the resulting posts. Produce ten distinct stories suitable for six social platforms. Write in British English.

Editorial accuracy: Kant includes duties of beneficence; do not claim compassion is forbidden. Distinguish emotional sympathy from acting on principle. Mill opposes social tyranny and distinguishes opinion from incitement; liberty is not absolute. Arendt’s portrayal of thoughtlessness is contested and never an excuse for genocide or individual guilt. Beauvoir’s situated freedom needs material and collective conditions, not willpower alone. Keep philosophical interpretations qualified rather than treating the grid as proof.

Recognisable subjects: every cover hook must name the thinker or book within 12 words; the first video beat must also name the thinker or book. Start every platform caption with a specific reference to that work, character, or thinker. Use concrete scenes and arguments, not generic inspirational advice. Avoid direct quotations; paraphrase carefully.
